39: This plan describes a counter-service taco shop with a gas-fired trompo in plain view and a salsa bar, in a mid-sized American city of 150,000 to 300,000 people. The trompo is the vertical broiler where al pastor is cooked: pork marinated in a chile and achiote adobo, stacked on a spit and turning where guests can see it from the street. The space is about 1,200 sq ft (111 sq m), with a Type I hood and an exhaust duct to the roof that is the filter for the whole business, {{aforo}} indoor seats and a 12-seat patio from April to October, and it is leased as a second-generation restaurant space on a street with foot traffic. It is run by a single-owner LLC: you as head taquero, the person who runs the trompo, and general manager, plus your team. Guests order at the counter; there is no table service. It opens in January, Tuesday through Sunday, for lunch and dinner, and closes on Mondays. The craft already has an audience: according to DataForSEO, Google US shows about 27,100 monthly searches for trompo and 74,000 for street tacos.
40: The key figures of the example case are these. We average {{clientes_dia}} covers a day across the counter, the patio, take-out and delivery, at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, over {{dias}} opening days. That produces {{ventas_a1}} in year-1 revenue and a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}}, or {{margen_neto_a1}} of sales. The average includes the ramp-up: the Excel spreads the year month by month, and Month 1 is January, one of the softest months, so the start falls on the low part of the year. Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, and cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}}. That is a modest net margin, and we would rather show you an honest number than a flattering one. It is not a guaranteed return but a starting point: change the assumptions and enter your own figures.
41: Total startup investment is {{inversion_total}}: {{capex}} for build-out, hood, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus a {{fondo_maniobra}} working capital reserve. The cash needed at opening comes to {{necesidad_caja}}. It is funded with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the total) and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period. The annual loan payment is {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
42: From there, covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3 at the same average check, so revenue rises to {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}, and net profit to {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}. The margin of safety over cash break-even is {{holgura_caja_pct}} in year 1, and the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) never falls below {{dscr_min}} over the life of the loan, against the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders typically look for. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow in the Excel: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone.
43: The team is small and leans on you. You are the head taquero and you run the trompo every day. With you are a line cook on the trompo and griddle, a prep cook for marinades, carnitas and salsas, a counter lead who also works the register, part-time counter and expo staff, dish and prep help and relief cover: {{plantilla_puestos}} people on the payroll who add up to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, all W-2 employees. The kit includes this ten-section business plan, the nine-sheet financial projections in Excel, the 80-task startup checklist in six phases, the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator and the Equivalents Guide. What sets it apart is trompo yield with real numbers: about 208 tacos from a 30 lb (13.6 kg) cone in the example, a kit estimate that you measure yourself.
46: Not every taco shop is the same business, and it pays to choose before you sign anything. The small counter-service shop built on a flat-top griddle and a comal (the flat surface where tortillas are heated), without a trompo, fits in far less space with fewer seats and a lower check: thin margin and no signature piece. The shop with a trompo and a salsa bar, which is the model in this plan, can be seen from the street. The full-service Mexican restaurant with a full bar is a different business, with a different license, check and staff, and it needs a restaurant business plan. The taco truck is another model, with its own commissary and permits, and it has its own kit: the Food Truck Business Plan Kit. At the extremes are the high-volume shop with rock-bottom prices and long lines, and the chef-driven shop with a very high price per taco. Each model has its own investment, space and margin, and this plan takes the middle one because it builds a product that is yours.
47: The value proposition is al pastor from a trompo in plain view, on corn tortillas made from nixtamalized corn (corn cooked with slaked lime), and a short menu of 8 to 10 street tacos. Each street taco comes on a double 6 in (15 cm) corn tortilla with onion and cilantro, which is what ordering it "with everything" means. You order by the plate: an order of 3 tacos of the same filling, or a combo plate with rice and beans. Next to the al pastor are carnitas (slow-cooked pork) and the stews of the day, plus gringas, which are a flour tortilla with al pastor and cheese, and the occasional campechano, a mix of two meats, or suadero, a soft slow-cooked beef cut. Birria on weekends is an option. The salsa bar runs on written rules, the aguas frescas (fresh fruit or hibiscus waters, lightly sweetened) are made in-house, and a build-your-own take-out order, with the tortillas and the filling packed apart, is how you send tacos home without them going soft.
48: The case prices to the market rather than to a wish. As a kit estimate based on the menus we reviewed, the street taco is $4.00, the plate of 3 tacos with rice and beans $14, the gringa or quesadilla $11.50, chips and guacamole $7, an aguas frescas (16 oz) $4.00, a soda $3.00 and a Mexican beer $6.50, all before sales tax. The shop sells beer and wine only, with no full liquor, and the beer and wine license is applied for early and never counted on. Everything is costed taco by taco: a street taco al pastor costs about $1.00 in ingredients, a food cost of 25% on $4.00 (kit estimate), and that is what lets it sell at a casual price and still leave a margin.
49: The average check in the case is {{ticket}} per cover excluding sales tax, which is {{precio_menu}} with tax included. At the counter it is made up of about 2.6 tacos, a quesadilla or a side such as chips and guacamole, and a little under one drink per guest (0.85 in the case), mostly aguas frescas and sodas with some beer. Food makes up {{comida_pct}} of sales and beverages {{bebida_pct}}. Third-party delivery marketplaces carry {{plataforma_pct}} of sales, and the rest is the counter, the patio and direct pickup. At that check, cost of goods is {{cogs_pct}} of sales, which leaves a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}}, and prime cost, which is cost of goods plus labor, is {{prime_cost_pct}}.
50: A detail that saves you a headache is saying clearly what you are. This is a taco shop and a taqueria, not a Tex-Mex restaurant and not a burrito-and-nachos place: promising one thing and serving another loses the guests who know the cuisine best, and also the ones who are looking for a real taqueria. Say what is on the plate: name each filling, write corn tortilla on the menu and the website, and call the chips tortilla chips. Tell guests what is in each salsa, because salsa macha, a chile oil made with peanuts and sesame, belongs on the allergen sign. And do not promise gluten-free if the comal or the fryer is shared with flour tortillas: the honest line is "corn tortillas are naturally gluten-free; ask about our fryer and griddle".
53: Demand for tacos is better read through what people search for than through market-size estimates of doubtful origin, and we have none with a source here. According to DataForSEO, on October 28, 2026 Google US shows these monthly searches: birria tacos 550,000, horchata 301,000, street tacos 74,000, trompo 27,100, tortilla machine 2,400, salsa bar 2,400, al pastor trompo 880, vertical broiler 480 and tortilla press commercial 260. Read them as interest in the craft, not as sales: they say that guests look for these dishes, that the vocabulary no longer sounds strange, and that the trade searches for the equipment.
54: There is a curious gap between the person who eats and the person who opens. Consumers search a lot: taco shop gets 60,500 monthly searches and taqueria 201,000, but most of that is people looking for lunch nearby, not people planning a business. The person about to open searches very little: taco shop business plan, taqueria business plan and how to open a taco shop get about 10 searches a month each, and mexican restaurant business plan about 20. It is an audience that decides with data and finds almost nothing made for its case.
55: On prices, the menus we reviewed in October 2026 put the street taco at roughly $3.00-3.75 in mid-sized cities and around $5 in large cities. That is a kit estimate: we could not confirm a full mid-sized-city menu, so check the ones in your area before you set yours. The case puts the street taco at $4.00 on the menu, which is what a new shop with a trompo in view needs to charge at 2026 costs: a little above the mid-sized band and well under big-city prices. Treat it as a reference, not a rule, because your neighborhood may pay more or less.
56: With Month 1 in January, the plan spreads sales with seasonality. May is the peak, with Cinco de Mayo and the patio, and the patio lifts every month from April to October; January and February are the softest months of the year. The Excel shows the spread between the best and the worst month: a neighborhood taco shop is a fairly flat business. Month 1 in January has a consequence: the ramp-up falls on January and February, the softest months, and that is why the working capital reserve counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row.
57: The gap is clear. What shows up on Google for taco shop business plan is a free generic restaurant template, taco truck guides, franchise pages and a paid plan for a street taco stand. None of them combines a fixed-location taco shop with a Word plan, an Excel that recalculates, a calculator for taco cost and trompo yield, and a checklist. Nobody counts trompo yield with numbers, the temperature your county sets for al pastor and for cut tomatoes, salsa macha on the allergen sign, bought tortillas versus making your own, or the chile distributor as a risk. This plan does, with an Excel you can change.
58: Demand carries risks that the plan names. A price war with the high-volume taquerias and the fast-casual chains puts pressure on the check. Marketplaces, with their commissions, eat your margin if you let them grow past the cap in the plan: the case carries {{plataforma_pct}} of sales at a commission of {{comision_pct}}. And depending on a single supplier of dried chiles is a weak point: if it fails, the salsas and the adobo fail with it. That is why the menu is short, pickup at the shop is pushed with price and it pays to keep a second Mexican specialty distributor on hand.
61: Before you set any price, draw the map of who competes with you in your neighborhood and your city. In tacos the competition comes from seven sides: high-volume taquerias, casual city taquerias, chef-driven taco shops, sit-down Mexican restaurants with a full bar, fast-casual and drive-thru Mexican chains, delivery-only kitchens, and the gyro and shawarma shop, which shares the vertical spit and the quick-dinner guest.
62: Porter's five forces look like this in a taco shop. Supplier power is moderate: corn tortillas, meat and produce can be bought in many places, but dried chiles depend on a few specialty distributors, and a failure shows up right away in the salsas and the adobo. Buyer power is high, because guests switch shops or apps with one tap and compare prices. The threat of new entrants is medium: opening a taco shop looks easy, but with a trompo the barrier is a space that can take a Type I hood and the craft of running the spit well. The threat of substitutes is high, because a guest can eat a burger, a chain burrito or a gyro. Rivalry is intense, with the price war of the volume shops. The defense is the trompo in view, the corn tortilla, the salsa bar and a neighborhood that comes back.
63: The direct competitors are the high-volume taquerias, with rock-bottom prices, lines and fast turns, and the casual city taquerias. Behind them come the chef-driven shops, with a very high price per taco and reservations, and the sit-down Mexican restaurants with a full bar. On the substitute side are the fast-casual Mexican chains, delivery-only kitchens and the gyro and shawarma shops. Your edge is the trompo in view, the corn tortilla, the salsa bar, a casual price with an order of 3 tacos or a plate, the build-your-own take-out order and a short menu costed taco by taco.
64: The barriers to entry are compliance and cash. Opening means plan review, a health permit and a pre-opening inspection, a building permit, a certificate of occupancy and a business license, plus a beer and wine license from the state and the city that can take months. The space is the filter: a gas trompo, a griddle and a fryer need a Type I hood with fire suppression (UL 300) and makeup air, and if the building cannot take the duct to the roof, the concept does not fit. Ask the fire marshal in writing, because NFPA 96 and your local fire and mechanical code decide. Add the patio permit and the investment in build-out, kitchen and hood. Check everything with your city before you sign the lease.
65: Four factors decide whether it works. The first is the product: al pastor from the trompo, well cooked and the same every day, a good corn tortilla and a short menu that executes fast. The second is the site: a street with foot traffic near a campus or a nightlife area, a space that can take a hood and its duct, and a patio that helps from April to October. The third is cost control: taco costing for every item and the yield of the trompo, which you measure and do not assume. The fourth is the team: a steady head taquero and a counter crew that looks after guests, because a neighbor's recommendation sells more than any ad.
66: The SWOT of this concept is clear. Strengths: a trompo in view, corn tortillas, a salsa bar, a casual price and a gross margin of {{margen_bruto_pct}} in year 1. Weaknesses: a space with hood requirements, dependence on one chile distributor and a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} that leaves little room for mistakes. Opportunities: a craft that people search for a lot, the campus and nightlife crowd, Cinco de Mayo and the build-your-own take-out order. Threats: the price war with the volume shops and marketplace commissions. The defense for each weak point lies in the product, the counter crew and pickup at the shop.
69: The marketing strategy starts in the neighborhood and follows the calendar. You open in January, and it helps to be clear about what to expect: the curious come the first month and the regulars take a quarter to build. That is why the plan does not count on a full house from day one but on a ramp. During that ramp three things carry the message: the trompo in view, which explains itself from the street, al pastor at a casual price, and service that makes people who walk in come back. Everything else, social media, the Google profile, combos and the stamp card, is there to turn that first visit into a second one.
70: Social media, and Instagram above all, is the showcase for the trompo. Post the building of the cone, the cut of the al pastor and the taco of the week. Short videos work better than menu photos: the trompo turning, the hand slicing and the taco being built in front of the camera. Show the salsa bar too, what each salsa tastes like and how hot it is, because that is the part that makes a first-timer hesitate. You do not need to post every day: a frequency you can keep is better than an opening burst that fades.
71: Your Google Business Profile is your best free ad, because nearly everyone looking for a taco shop nearby checks it. Complete it with photos of the trompo, the salsa bar, the counter and the patio, and keep the lunch and dinner hours current, Tuesday through Sunday, including the Monday closure. Claim your Yelp page too. Reply to every review, the bad ones as well, in a calm tone and with the name of the shop. A careful reply reads like a commitment, and it counts for the guest who has not visited yet.
72: Local outreach starts at your door. The campus and nightlife crowd is your natural guest, and lunch combos are the simple way to win those people and fill weekday lunch. Through the year the calendar gives you two dates to work with: Taco Tuesday every week and Cinco de Mayo, which is celebrated mostly in the United States, without inventing more. And to bring guests back, keep it simple: a stamp card, on paper or on a phone. You do not need to promise conversion numbers you do not have: start with the card, measure how many get completed and adjust.
73: Marketplace or in-house delivery is a numbers decision. The plan sells {{plataforma_pct}} of its sales through third-party delivery marketplaces and pays a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders. Published tiers run from 15% to 30% on DoorDash and from 20% to 30% on Uber Eats, with Grubhub's marketing and delivery fees on top, plus promotions and packaging. Your own driver costs wages, employer payroll taxes, hired and non-owned auto insurance and fuel, and in most states must be a W-2 employee, so check your state. It tends to pay only with your own orders or a short, dense delivery zone, and it carries labor risk without the marketplace's storefront.
74: Pickup at the shop pays no commission, so push it with price. A small discount on an order that is picked up costs less than the marketplace commission and brings the guest to your door, where he or she sees the trompo and may order something more. There is a product problem with delivery too: the tortilla arrives worse after the ride. The build-your-own order, with the tortillas and the filling packed apart, holds up, and a short delivery radius helps, which is why the plan's ceiling is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales through marketplaces. There is no in-house delivery in the plan: if you ever set one up, do it with the numbers above in front of you.
75: The marketing budget in the case is {{marketing_anual}} a year, mostly for photography, local ads and the materials for the combos. The brand, website, photos and launch are separate, inside the startup costs ({{inv_lanzamiento}}). Do not spend it all at once: spread it with the calendar and keep part for the softest months, January and February.
